title: Forestry stocks: how to analyze forestry companies
description: Forestry stocks: cycle leverage, the gross margin staircase 12–69 percent, four of five companies below book value — with the universe's own numbers.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Forestry stocks are shares in companies that own forest land and refine wood into pulp, paper and packaging. In AK1A's universe the family holds five companies with complete four-year series: SCA, Holmen and Billerud in Sweden, and Stora Enso and UPM in Finland. The valuation rests on three legs — the biological tree growing independently of the business cycle, the factory refining it, and the balance sheet carrying both through the cycle's bottom years. The craft therefore differs from that for growth and service companies: leverage, degree of integration and book value do the work. This guide walks through the mechanisms with the universe's own numbers (raw data 2026-09-03) — education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What are forestry stocks — the tree, the pulp and the package

The business is a chain: the forest is harvested, timber becomes pulp, pulp becomes paper or packaging material. That gives two revenue engines. The first is the timber itself — a raw material whose price swings with demand for sawlogs, pulp and energy, set on a global market where Nordic companies are price takers rather than price makers. The second is refining — factories profitable only when the product price exceeds the fixed cost. Companies owning large forest land also get biological growth in the base: the forest grows every year, even when the market does not pay, and the standing timber becomes a buffer no factory can build. Around the chain lies a third leg, energy — byproducts like chips and bark, and the black liquor becoming electricity and heat as the pulp cooks. [The National Forest Inventory](https://www.slu.se/srh), SLU's annual survey of Sweden's forests since 1923, is the industry's reference for how condition, growth and harvesting develop.

Against earlier guides: the commodity cycle guide treats the whole materials branch (mining, steel, forest) at cycle level — here we enter the forest family's own mechanics. And forest land is not a rental property: it competes with no one for tenants, but produces timber on its own biological clock.

## The cycle's leverage — when revenue fell six percent, earnings fell 55

The Swedish companies' series for 2022–2023 show the industry's core mechanism. Add up SCA, Holmen and Billerud: revenue fell from 87.3 to 82.1 billion kronor — roughly six percent. Earnings fell in the same turn from 17.3 to 7.8 billion — roughly 55 percent. Revenue dropped by one twentieth; earnings more than halved. That is [cycle risk's](/kurser/rk-05-cykelrisk) operating leverage in reality: factories, forests and logistics cost almost as much in a weak year as a strong one, so every krona lost in the price strikes straight through to earnings — here roughly nine times harder than on the revenue side.

The individual companies sharpen the picture. SCA's earnings fell from 6,821 to 3,625 million kronor — nearly halved. Billerud fell from 4,590 to 484 million — close to 90 percent. UPM lost three quarters (1,526 to 388 million euro) and Holmen just over a third (5,874 to 3,697 million kronor). Stora Enso went from a 1,536 million euro profit to a 357 million loss. Same year, five companies, same direction — an industry cycle, not a company miss.

Then lay your hand on the 2025 earnings and read the cycle's position: SCA 3,205 million kronor (the top year 2022: 6,821), Holmen 2,879 (5,874), Billerud 711 (4,590), Stora Enso 695 million euro (after two loss years) and UPM 480 (1,526). None is back at the top, none remains at the bottom — the recovery has begun but is not complete. [The margin staircase's mechanics](/kurser/ln-03-marginaltrappan-och-operativ-havstavng) explain why a price improvement of a few percent moves earnings by tens of percent: the leverage that struck downward in 2023 strikes upward when the cycle turns.

## The degree of integration — the gross margin staircase from 12 to 69 percent

The industry's [gross margins](/kurser/v07-bruttomarginal) form a staircase with a span of more than 57 percentage points: SCA 69.4, Billerud 46.1, Holmen 45.6, Stora Enso 24.7 and UPM 12.2 percent. The staircase tells where in the chain each company books its revenue. An integrated company with its own forest transfers timber to its own pulp at internal cost — the raw material never shows in cost of goods. A purchasing-driven company carries the timber price as a cost item directly in the income statement, and the gross margin falls mechanically.

But gross margin alone says nothing about profitability — compare [the EBIT margins](/kurser/ln-05-vad-ar-lonsamhet) in the same turn: SCA carries 3.9 percent and UPM 9.8 — the group's highest. The high gross covers a heavy refining apparatus; the low gross rests on a narrower cost base. So read the staircase: gross shows the place in the chain, EBIT what the refining leaves behind. [Return on invested capital](/kurser/roic-01-avkastning-pa-investerat-kapital) varies sharply: negative for Billerud after the bottom year, 0.8 percent for SCA, at most 6.8 percent for UPM — a capital-heavy industry in the cycle's bottom layer, where invested capital works at low gearing.

## The balance sheet — four of five companies below book value

Price per book equity: Billerud 0.72, Stora Enso 0.74, SCA 0.80, Holmen 0.91 and UPM 1.28 — median 0.80, with four of five below 1.0. The market thus prices the group below its [balance sheet value](/kurser/bk-01-balansrakningen). One classic explanation: forest land is booked at old acquisition values while the biological capital grows on the root. Another, less friendly: the industry's return lies below the cost of capital at the bottom of the cycle — then book value is a floor in theory but not a price in practice. [The debt-to-equity ratio](/kurser/v10-skuldsattningsgrad) holds the group up through it: 0.13 to 0.38 in debt per equity krona is low even for a cyclical industry, and it is why all five could carry the 2023 loss years without issuing new shares — the capital structure is the family's built-in crisis insurance.

## The multiple traps — P/E 36 at the bottom of the cycle

Cyclical companies destroy naive multiple comparisons. SCA trades at a [P/E](/kurser/km-009-pe) of 36.5 — while [return on equity](/blogg/v09-roe-analys) is 2.2 percent. The multiple is not expensive in itself; the earnings are small. Billerud lacks a P/E entirely (negative earnings) but carries a PEG of 4.03 against consensus growth above 370 percent — percent growth from nearly zero earnings becomes astronomical without saying anything about future earnings power, one of [the PEG multiple's weaknesses](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026). Stora Enso looks cheap at a P/E of 14.1 — the same small-earnings-high-multiple effect from the other direction.

The craft is the normal-year earnings — a rough measure suffices: the average of a top year and a bottom year. For the Swedish companies' 2022 and 2023 earnings that becomes (17.3 + 7.8) divided by two, about 12.5 billion kronor. The actual 2025 level — 6.8 billion for the same three companies — still lies about 46 percent below that rough normal year. That is the distance the cycle has left to travel, and it is against the normal year [the relative valuation](/kurser/km-011-relativ-vardering) should be calculated — not against bottom-year earnings, not against the consensus percent. Compare against [the industry medians](/blogg/branschmedianer-akm2) rather than a market index.

## The checklist — five steps when you analyze forestry stocks

1. **Draw the leverage.** Lay revenue and earnings series for 2022–2025 side by side. The ratio between the declines (here six against 55 percent) is the industry's signature.
2. **Read gross and EBIT together.** The 12–69 percent staircase in gross shows chain position; the EBIT margin shows what that position is worth.
3. **Examine the balance sheet through the cycle.** Debt-to-equity below roughly 0.5 and intact cash flows in the bottom year separate survivors from expected share issues.
4. **Calculate on a normal year.** The multiple against the bottom year's earnings (P/E 36) or the spike in the consensus percent (PEG at +370) leads astray — use the cycle average.
5. **Follow the industry's statistics.** The Swedish Forest Agency's harvest and price statistics, the Forest Industries' data and the National Forest Inventory's growth measurements provide the foundation beyond the share price.

So a forestry analysis is built: leverage first, degree of integration next, the balance sheet as gate and the normal year as price. For a deeper walkthrough there is [the Forest Sector's methodology](/kurser/se-17-skogssektorn), [the sector analysis method](/kurser/se-16-sektoranalysens-metod) and [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026).

_Sources: AK1A's 256-company universe (Yahoo Finance/MarketStack, raw data 2026-09-03); [the Swedish Forest Industries Federation](https://skogsindustrierna.se); [the Swedish Forest Agency](https://www.skogsstyrelsen.se); [SLU National Forest Inventory](https://www.slu.se/srh)._

_This is educational financial analysis, not investment advice._
